entry.title: GitHub Availability Report: October 2026
entry.content:
We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes)

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

What went wrong and why?

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How did we respond?

  1. A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up.
  2. Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident.
  3. We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue.
  4. We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover.
  5. We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it.
  • We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded.
  • We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time.
  • We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on.

October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes)

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

What went wrong and why?

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How did we respond?

  1. A surge of migration work overloaded a shared database, causing requests across github.com to fail or slow down.
  2. Automated monitoring detected the failures and paged our on-call engineers.
  3. The errors stopped on their own within minutes.
  4. We declared an incident and paused enterprise migrations to prevent a recurrence while we investigated the cause.
  5. Once a mitigation was deployed, we resumed migrations and resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We optimized the query GitHub Enterprise Importer sends to the database so that each one stays small and fixed in size.
  • We are automating importer backoff when the database is under strain, easing load before it can affect other GitHub services.
  • We are adding database alerts that flag queries doing much more work than usual and identify which query is responsible, so we can find and fix problems like this one faster.

October 07 15:14 and 17:17 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 11 minutes, and 47 minutes, respectively)

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

What went wrong and why?

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How did we respond?

  1. Automated monitoring alerted us to failing writes, and we declared an incident.
  2. Writes recovered when an established machine with correct records became leader and published correct settings.
  3. We traced the cause to the new machine, resolved the first incident, and paused automated maintenance to prevent a repeat.
  4. When a maintenance task did not honor the pause and the outage repeated, we declared a second incident.
  5. Writes recovered when an established machine became leader again. We removed the new machine and resolved the second incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We improved how we retire database servers, so outdated records aren’t left behind.
  • We tightened controls on adding new machines that manage database routing, and making sure automated maintenance honors a pause.
  • We strengthened validation of database routing settings, so incorrect settings are caught before they take effect.

October 19 15:49 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 7 minutes)

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

What went wrong and why?

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How did we respond?

  1. Automated alerts detected the failures, we declared an incident, and we traced the problem to the shared network link.
  2. We routed the actions service away from some of its cache servers in that region, but the link was still over capacity.
  3. We routed it away from the rest of those cache servers, and the link recovered.
  4. We raised processing limits to clear the actions backlog, and we resolved the incident once all affected services had recovered.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We have limited how quickly this actions service can open new connections to its cache servers.
  • We are alerting on spikes in new connections from this service to identify and address the source sooner.

October 21 14:52 UTC (lasting 4 hours and 30 minutes)

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

What went wrong and why?

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How did we respond?

  1. We declared an incident and moved some traffic off an overloaded server, but more servers became overloaded soon after.
  2. We split the busiest traffic into more partitions and moved it to less-loaded servers. All affected features except audit logs gradually recovered.
  3. Once the audit log service stopped restarting, we raised the rate at which it could write events so the backlog would clear faster.
  4. We resolved the incident once audit log delays were back within the healthy range, and the remaining backlog cleared afterward.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We added randomized delays to reconnects after a failed request, so servers that are already slow don’t get hit with a burst of new connections.
  • We are alerting earlier on server memory use, so we can move traffic before a server slows down.
  • We are adding a second destination for webhook delivery data that we can switch to, so we can keep webhook deliveries moving if our event streaming platform slows down.
  • We have improved our playbooks to move hot partitions for similar situations in the future

October 28 14:12 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 16 minutes)

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

What went wrong and why?

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How did we respond?

  1. A credential we use with an upstream model provider stopped working, and requests to the affected models began to fail.
  2. Alerts flagged rising errors on the affected models, and we declared an incident.
  3. We posted a public status update and recommended choosing another model in the meantime.
  4. We traced the errors to our own credential and created a replacement.
  5. We began deploying the new credential, and requests started to recover once the first environment was updated.
  6. We completed the deployment in the remaining environments, confirmed that requests to the affected models had recovered, and resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We improved how our service handles authentication failures from upstream model providers, so requests can be retried instead of failing.
  • We are strengthening how we manage credentials for upstream model providers.
  • We are adding alerts for authentication failures from upstream model providers, so we can identify and address this kind of problem faster.

October 30 14:31 UTC (lasting 31 minutes)

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

What went wrong and why?

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How did we respond?

  1. Requests used up every connection in the shared database pool, and requests across github.com began to fail.
  2. We declared an incident after seeing failures, and on-call engineers for the affected services were paged.
  3. The pool drained and error rates returned to normal. Shortly after, we confirmed that the full connection pool had caused the errors and posted a public status update.
  4. We verified that database connections were back to normal and resolved the incident after monitoring for stability.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We are now running the slow lookup before these update requests start writing a change, so they no longer hold a database connection while they wait.
  • We are evaluating limits on how long a pooled database connection can be held, so a slow request pattern is less likely to tie up the pool.

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

The post GitHub availability report: October 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

entry.title: 价值6个亿！阿维塔1300台战损测试车曝光：总裁现场砸宁德时 代电池不坏
entry.content:
快科技11月12日消息，阿维塔官方今日直击废车场现场，1300台战损测试车集中曝光，总价值6亿元。

阿维塔总裁雍军在现场亲自抡锤砸宁德时代整包电池，砸后电池未损坏，以此重申全系100%采用宁德时代高安全电池、绝不混装的承诺。

测试中多次要求加重力度，观察电池包受砸后的空间挤压和震手感，砸后整包电池完好无损。

测试台架保留至次日，开放给现场参与者亲身体验。雍军强调，阿维塔所有的价值都是为客户创造价值，用户开心了团队就开心。

这片废车场停放的1300台战损车，全部为完成全部测试流程的试验样车，测完即报废，不流入终端市场。

雍军此前在11月10日在社交平台上发文回应“价值6个亿的废车场”争议时表示，这些战损车对阿维塔来说非常重要，不仅因为这些车不便宜，更因为它们的共同点是都不能卖给用户。

雍军介绍，在交到用户手里之前，每一台车都要经历大量严苛的测试，涵盖整车耐久、高温、低温、强化腐蚀、复杂路面冲击、涉水、碰撞安全、无框车门开合耐久等多个项目。

有些车要经历“两冬两夏”，有些车要在极寒、极热环境下反复验证，有些车要跑几十万公里，有些车甚至要经历破坏性测试，部分测试做完车就直接报废了。

“这些投入确实不小，但我始终觉得这些钱花得值，汽车研发没有捷径，研发测试的钱一分都不能省。”雍军称，阿维塔坚决不造速成车，车一旦速成，一个家庭没了的可能性就会增大。

“造车不是赶时间，而是对得起每一份托付。车可以晚一点交付，但安全，永远不能有一点侥幸。”

11月9日的阿维塔“全球首拆”直播中，雍军已给出两项硬承诺：全系100%采用宁德时代高安全电池，绝不混装；华为896线双光路激光雷达不减配。

entry.title: Build Once, Run on Any Agent: A Practical Guide to Agent Skills
entry.content:
How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

Define one job and when it applies

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

---name: proof-agentdescription: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues.---

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

Keep project configuration out of the skill

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

project:  name: "support-desk"  store_name: "support_metric_store"
platform:
  engine: “duckdb”
  pipeline_framework: “spark_python”
  duckdb_dir: “warehouse”

<clipboard-copy aria-label=”Copy” class=”code-copy-btn” data-copy-feedback=”Copied!” role=”button” tabindex=”0” value=’project:
name: “support-desk”
store_name: “support_metric_store”

platform:
engine: “duckdb”
pipeline_framework: “spark_python”
duckdb_dir: “warehouse”‘>

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

Share execution paths between skills

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

Put checks and approval points in the workflow

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Package for each agent client, then verify its setup

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

node scripts/package.mjs --check

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Three practices for building agent skills

  1. Put business context in one file. Keep project-specific names, schemas, and conventions in a manifest, and have each skill read it instead of duplicating those facts. This gives the team one visible place to update configuration.
  2. Give related skills one consistent way to use the platform. Have related skills use the same path to run queries, jobs, and schema changes instead of each defining its own commands and connection logic. This makes the workflow’s access easier to understand and its behavior easier to check in each client.
  3. Use instructions to guide the work, and checks to verify it. A skill can tell an agent which standards to follow and when to ask for approval. Add human review at decisions that need context or judgment, and use tests and CI checks to catch issues before a change moves forward. If a check must block a merge or deployment, configure that requirement in your repository’s rules.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

Add an agent skill to GitHub Copilot >

The post Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

entry.title: 支付宝新一代碰一下终端首发：能碰能扫码 还能刷境内外银行卡
entry.content:
快科技11月12日消息，支付宝官方宣布，中国银联与蚂蚁集团联合研发推广的“全功能融合创新终端”今日在银泰商业西安钟楼开元商城全国首发，银联商务作为授权经销商和运营方，已在国内落地首批标杆项目。

这款终端是当前市场上支付方式兼容维度最全面的金融级智能POS终端，同时满足银联企业技术规范和支付宝IoT设备安全规范，可实现支付宝“碰一下”、境内外银行卡、二维码聚合支付、手机Pay、数字人民币等主流支付方式一机通收。

针对商户多机收银、操作繁琐的经营难题，终端以“一机替代多设备”压缩硬件采购、设备维护与多系统对账成本，入境游客、老年人和视障人群也能选择更适合自己的方式付款。

在收银之外，终端还叠加了数字化经营能力，支持合并支付及资金分账，适配多供货商联营、连锁门店等业态。

集成电子发票云服务与“即买即退”等离境退税功能，同时可一站式受理国家“以旧换新”等促消费业务。

支付宝介绍，“碰一下”自2024年7月推出以来，已覆盖点餐、出行等2200个细分场景，接入3000万个线下点位，服务4亿用户，全功能融合终端则把这一生态从设备、线圈贴纸扩展到融合POS形态。

entry.title: 京东双11手机销量榜：苹果小米抢尽风头 iPhone霸榜前4
entry.content:
快科技11月12日消息，双11手机谁卖得好？从京东手机竞速排行榜来看，苹果包揽单品累计总榜前4，小米则拿下3000元以下、3000-4999元2个价位段的冠军。

这组榜单的统计时间为11月11日23时36分至23时39分，并非活动结束后的最终排名，但已经能看出临近收官时的竞争情况。

总榜冠军是iPhone 18 Pro Max，紧随其后的是iPhone 17、iPhone 18 Pro和iPhone 17 Pro。新款、老款一起上榜，苹果直接占住前4个位置。

小米也拿走了总榜前10中的3个席位。REDMI Note 17 Pro排名第5，REDMI K100 Pro Max排名第7，REDMI K90至尊版排名第8。

剩下3个位置，分别属于排名第6的荣耀X80 Pro Max、第9的荣耀X70焕新版，以及第10的华为畅享90 Pro Max。

分价位来看，苹果在7000元以上榜单中更强势，前5全部是iPhone，依次为iPhone 18 Pro Max、iPhone 18 Pro、iPhone 17 Pro、iPhone 17 Pro Max和iPhone Duo。

到了5000-6999元档，iPhone 17继续拿下第1，华为Mate 80、一加16分列第2、第3。小米17 Pro Max排在第9，这个价位段的品牌分布更分散。

小米的优势则集中在5000元以下。3000-4999元榜单中，REDMI K100 Pro Max夺冠，荣耀WINRT2、iQOO Z11 Turbo紧随其后。小米MIXFlip2、REDMI K100 Pro和小米17 Pro也进入前10，小米共占4席。

3000元以下，REDMI Note 17 Pro排名第1，荣耀X80 Pro Max排名第2，REDMI K90至尊版排名第3。加上REDMI K100和REDMI Note 17，小米同样占据4席。

entry.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an Unusual Consensus Algorithm
entry.content:
Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.  

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

  • Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.
  • Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.
  • Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.
  • Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.  

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round:  After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithmhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/choosing-quepaxa/

entry.title: 均价超50万！享界G9产能爬坡顺利：本月交付可冲5000台
entry.content:
快科技11月9日消息，鸿蒙智行旗下高端硬派豪华SUV享界G9产能爬坡迎来关键进展，据品牌产品总监对外披露，该车终端成交均价已经突破50万元，11月首周ToC端交付量达到1435台，全月目标冲击5000台交付量。

享界G9于9月底才启动首批交付，10月是完整生产交付首月，前期经历了一段产能爬坡周期，依托享界超级工厂升级后的柔性产线，生产效率持续提升，订单转化速度明显加快。

该车官方指导价区间42.98万-54.98万元，订单里高配版本占比极高，Ultra、Ultra+高端配置订单占九成，直接拉高整车成交均价，用户画像也偏向豪华车增换购群体，不少来自奔驰、宝马、路虎等传统豪华品牌车主。

作为北汽与华为联合打造的全新车型，享界G9长宽高为5206（5377）*2050*1897mm，轴距3160mm，定位全尺寸SUV，有五座、六座版本可选。

全系标配38个传感器，包括华为896线激光雷达、三固态激光雷达，支持全场景辅助系统，并拥有全链路八大冗余，满足L3自动驾驶的架构需求。

首发华为全地形图灵平台，配备双阀连续可变阻尼减振器、集中供气双腔空气悬架、800mm涉水深度、透明底盘以及±12°后轮转向。

同时首发了鸿蒙智行智能全地形系统、800V全主动可断开稳定杆、自适应差速锁以及华为智擎800V高效动力平台。

提供增程、纯电两种动力，标配800V高压碳化硅动力平台，前后双电机四驱，系统功率437千瓦，并配备56/75kWh（增程）和120kWh（纯电）电池，对应CLTC纯电续航310km、405km以及701/728km。

entry.title: 安卓涨价给了苹果顺水人情！iPhone 18 Pro想不火都难
entry.content:
博主RD观测公布了国内智能手机2026年第44周TOP30榜单，结果有点意思——iPhone 18 Pro系列直接包揽了销量榜前二，其中Pro Max完全是断层第一，跟第三名拉开了不小的差距。

前五名里苹果占了四席，第三是上一代iPhone 17，第四是折叠屏iPhoneDuo，第五是iPhone 17 Pro。整张榜单里苹果一共占了6款机型。国产机型排名最高的是华为Pura X View，列第六，然后是荣耀X80 Pro Max和华为畅享90 Pro Max。

这背后最有意思的反差就是安卓涨价，苹果卖爆。今年以来安卓旗舰普遍涨价，新一代旗舰起售价持续往上探，Pro级顶配版本普遍冲到六七千元，部分超高端机型定价直追苹果Pro系列，高配版本甚至逼近万元。但涨得越狠，用户跑得越快，直接跑到苹果那边去了。

当然，安卓涨价不是厂商想赚更多，是被逼的。TrendForce的数据显示，2026年一季度存储合约价格同比上涨接近200%，

存储在手机物料成本里的占比从原来的10%到15%，直接冲到了30%到40%。AI服务器抢走了大量内存和闪存产能，上游成本先炸了，下游卖价只能跟着涨，这事前几篇稿子也聊过。

苹果这边也不是躺赢，产品策略改得很准。标准版延后发售，原来预算只够买基础款的用户，要么等要么加预算，结果相当一部分被挤向了更贵的Pro档。

第三方数据显示，iPhone 18 Pro首销前三天销量同比增长12%，这个增幅在整个手机市场都在下滑的背景下，确实很亮眼。

最后一个推手是换机周期拉长。现在用户平均换机间隔已经突破了三年，越来越多的人不再追求频繁换新款，而是加预算一步到位，买体验更好、寿命更长的机型。

在高端市场的"一步到位"选项里，iPhone Pro系列凭借长期系统支持、稳定口碑和更高的二手保值率，一直是多数用户的优先选项。

说白了，安卓这次涨价反而是送了苹果一个顺水人情。本来苹果Pro系列的定价已经够高了，安卓旗舰一路追上来，直接打消了用户"等等安卓更便宜"的念头——既然都要花大价钱，不如一步到位买保值的苹果。这个逻辑不复杂，但足够把销量推向一边倒。

安卓涨价给了苹果顺水人情！iPhone 18 Pro想不火都难https://finance.sina.com.cn/tech/roll/2026-11-09/doc-iniyears6402987.shtml

entry.title: Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
entry.content:
Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.

When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.

Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.

AI is changing open source

AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.

The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.

During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.

AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.

Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.

One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.

Fund distribution

The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.

The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:

  • Contributions to ecosystem recipients
  • Stipends to core maintainers

We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.

We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter.

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward.

Stipends to core maintainers

The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month.

Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on.

Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible.

Cloudflare supports open source

Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it.

Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria.

The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

entry.title: 又一款阔折叠进行中：OPPO主打轻薄 独家无痕技术
entry.content:
快科技11月9日消息，在华为、苹果相继推出阔折叠形态的旗舰机型之后，其他主流手机厂商也纷纷跟进布局这类新品类，OPPO就是进度靠前的玩家之一。

现在有数码博主爆料称，OPPO正在推进自家首款阔折叠机型的研发落地，新机大概率会划归Find N产品线，最终命名很可能定为Find N7。

这款OPPO阔折叠新机搭载了独家的屏幕无痕折痕技术，整机核心主打极致轻薄的使用体验。影像配置上升级了一枚2亿像素主摄，同步搭载多光谱传感器，核心性能芯片选用台积电2nm工艺制程的骁龙旗舰芯。

按照之前供应链流出的规划信息，OPPO很可能会把Find N7做成覆盖多形态的完整产品系列，产品线阵容里同时包含常规大折叠版本和全新阔折叠版本，覆盖不同用户的使用偏好。

对于OPPO来说，研发阔折叠类产品并没有太强的陌生感，毕竟多年前他们推出的Find N2，凭借远优于行业平均水平的轻薄表现，完全可以看作当下阔折叠手机的技术鼻祖，在这类产品形态上已经沉淀了非常充足的调校经验。

阔折叠已经成为当前高端折叠屏市场增长最快的细分赛道，叠加华为、苹果头部玩家的产品教育，后续这条赛道的技术比拼很快就会从基础形态普及，直接升级到影像、性能、轻薄度等全方位体验的硬核对抗，整个折叠屏行业的产品迭代速度还会进一步加快。

从目前市场表现看，华为的阔折叠手机销售还是很不错的。

entry.title: 40万级没对手！问界M8上市19个月狂卖19万台：拿下细分市场第一
entry.content:
快科技11月9日消息，问界汽车官方今日宣布，家庭智慧旗舰SUV问界M8累计交付突破19万台，上市19个月获得上市周期40万级SUV销量第一、30至40万级新能源车型净推荐值（NPS）第一等多项市场标杆成绩。

问界M8于2025年4月16日首次上市，由赛力斯汽车与华为联合设计，定位家庭智慧旗舰SUV，搭载华为途灵平台和HUAWEI ADS智驾系统，提供五座版和六座版，官方指导价35.98万至44.98万元。

上市前便斩获15万辆订单，上市6个月累计交付超10万台，2026年4月16日一周年时交付突破17万台，位列40万级SUV年度销量榜首。如今上市19个月交付达19万台，平均月销破万。

问界新M8定档11月13日上市，10月30日已开放配置选择，推出Max、Max+、Ultra三个版本，预售区间38.98万至45.98万元。

官方表示新M8累计投入15亿元按全新车型标准开发，新增天幕青等车色、后轮转向和隔空关门功能，2026款全系搭载896线激光雷达。

智驾是这次升级的核心。问界新M8全系标配华为乾崑智驾ADS 5.4系统，搭载新一代全向立体融合感知系统，采用面向未来的L3级自动驾驶架构设计。

底盘和三电系统同样大幅升级。问界新M8全系切换到800V高压平台，纯电长续航版CLTC续航达830公里，增程顶配版综合续航1435公里。底盘方面配备全新调校智能底盘，搭载双腔双阀空气悬架和后轮转向系统，操控灵活性和乘坐舒适性都有提升。

座舱方面，新车提供三零重力座椅（六座车型适配），配备C形菱格光岛和交互智能氛围灯，搭载全新影音系统和专属智能座舱设计。外观方面新增天地万象车色和全新豪华轮毂，延续鲲鹏设计语言。

外观方面，新车提供全新天地万象车色、全新豪华轮毂和鲲鹏设计语言。内饰采用奢雅拼色方案，配备C形麦格光岛和交互智能氛围灯，内饰配色包含沙砾棕和澜月白两种选择。

entry.title: Beyond Code Generation: A Developer’s Guide to Agentic Engineering
entry.content:
This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

  • Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together.
  • Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately.
  • Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions.
  • Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

Build: Move more than one task forward at a time

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

  • Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you.
  • Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later.
  • Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree.
  • Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks.
  • Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time.
  • Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

Verify: Spend your attention where it counts

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

  • Stack up smaller, more focused pull requests instead of creating a single, massive change. You and your agents can use stacked pull requests to separate dependent work into smaller pieces. This lets each PR be reviewed on its own, keeps dependencies visible, and unblocks teams by letting them build on top of your work before it merges.
  • Catch routine quality issues before they consume review time. GitHub Code Quality checks changes against coding practices and your organization’s standards, catching issues before they reach a human reviewer and saving time for both authors and reviewers.
  • Get review help matched to the change. Copilot code review gives automated feedback, with lighter analysis for simple changes and deeper analysis for complex ones. You can set that depth yourself or let Copilot select it for each pull request.
  • Check security across more of your codebase. AI Scan finds vulnerabilities in languages and files beyond CodeQL’s coverage. AI secret detection helps identify unstructured secrets, such as passwords, that pattern matching can miss.
  • Keep new dependencies within policy. License compliance checks dependency licenses against your company’s rules before merging. GitHub package firewall, currently in public preview for npm, can block downloads that violate configured security policies.
  • Resolve findings and follow-up work without babysitting every pull request. Agentic Autofix proposes repairs for security issues, while Agent Merge automatically addresses failing checks, review comments, and merge conflicts—helping you keep your pull requests moving and preparing them for merge. And, if you configure it, Copilot will even merge your pull requests once your verification steps are passing.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Observe: Learn from what happens after you ship

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

  • Check assumptions against real behavior. With access to your observability tools and business data through connectors such as Fabric, Copilot can help investigate which requests or customer groups are affected.
  • Capture the finding where someone can act on it. Ask Copilot to draft an issue with supporting evidence and acceptance criteria, including a regression test for the failure you uncovered.
  • Carry useful lessons into future work. Review suggested improvements from Dreaming, which uses sessions and repository activity to help refine memories, skills, and code review guidance.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Where to start

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

Get started with Copilot >

The post Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
